contributions.headingText: Endometrioid carcinoma is a malignant epithelial neoplasm displaying varying proportions of glandular, papillary, and solid architecture, with the neoplastic cells showing endometrioid differentiation.

There are four molecular subtypes: POLE-ultramutated endometrioid carcinoma, mismatch repair–deficient endometrioid carcinoma, p53-mutant endometrioid carcinoma, and no specific molecular profile (NSMP) endometrioid carcinoma.

Endometrioid endometrial carcinoma (EEC) mostly affects postmenopausal women (90% > 50 years), with a median patient age of 63 years. Cases typically present with abnormal/postmenopausal bleeding. Advanced disease presents with pelvic/abdominal symptoms resembling those of ovarian carcinoma.

Endometrial cancer makes up the vast majority (80% in Europe {24120180} and > 90% in the USA) of corpus uteri malignancies; it is the sixth most commonly diagnosed cancer in women and the second most commonly diagnosed female genital organ cancer. It is estimated that about 382 000 women were diagnosed with corpus uteri cancer globally in 2018 and that age-standardized (World) incidence rates varied from 1 to 25 cases per 100 000 person-years {30207593}. The highest rates were found in very high Human Development Index (HDI) countries (where more than half of the cases occurred) and in central and eastern Europe (e.g. Belarus), and the lowest rates were found in low-HDI countries (e.g. Yemen, The Gambia, and Malawi) (see #13835Fig. #13835). In several countries, endometrial cancer incidence rates have been increasing over the past decades and in successive generations, especially in countries undergoing rapid socioeconomic transitions, such as China, Brazil, and South Africa {29045681}. Women who have had a hysterectomy are no longer at risk of developing uterine cancer. Failure to exclude them from the population at risk artificially lowers incidence rates {31116674}, but hysterectomy prevalence is seldom available for correcting the rates accordingly. Corpus uteri cancer is often diagnosed after menopause and at an early stage, following bleeding. In high-income countries, the 5-year survival rate is high (~80% in the USA). Worldwide, corpus uteri cancer is the 14th leading cause of cancer death, with close to 90 000 deaths per year. The estimated age-standardized mortality rates for 2018 range from < 1 death per 100 000 person-years (in the countries with the lowest incidence) to 6 per 100 000 in the countries with high incidence or intermediate incidence and limited access to care {30207593}.
Prolonged exposure to unopposed estrogen is a risk factor.

There are shared molecular alterations with endometrial atypical hyperplasia / endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia. An increased risk is conferred by exposure to higher total concentrations of estrogens, such as with early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, obesity, tamoxifen, polycystic ovary syndrome, or estrogen-producing ovarian tumours {24463639; 19554665}. There is an association with Lynch syndrome and Cowden syndrome {29287922}.
The tumours are exophytic or diffusely infiltrative. Varying degrees of necrosis and haemorrhage can be seen. Some cases arise within the lower uterine segment.

EEC typically displays (villo)glandular architecture, composed of cells that are usually columnar with pseudostratified nuclei. These (villo)glandular structures typically show a smooth luminal outline. The cytoplasm of the neoplastic cells is usually eosinophilic and granular. Nuclear atypia is mild to moderate, with inconspicuous nucleoli, except in high-grade EEC. The mitotic count is highly variable. Squamous differentiation is frequent (occuring in 10–25% of cases), manifesting as morules or as solid sheets of eosinophilic cells and even with keratinization. Histological patterns, which are not associated with different prognosis, include secretory patterns (resembling those of early secretory endometrium, either focal or diffuse, mimicking clear cell carcinoma), small non-villous papillae, microglandular pattern, spindle cell pattern, sertoliform pattern, and sex cord–like formations and hyalinization. Mucinous pattern may be present in varying degrees and may predominate.

The distinction of well-differentiated EEC from endometrial atypical hyperplasia / endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia is based on the presence of stromal invasion, which is defined by loss of intervening stroma (a confluent glandular, cribriform, or maze-like pattern), an altered endometrial stroma (desmoplastic stromal reaction), or a complex (mostly villoglandular) architecture. EEC with mucinous differentiation may be difficult to distinguish from atypical mucinous glandular proliferations; cribriform or confluent architecture and cytological atypia are distinguishing features {10619266}.

Grading

EEC is graded using FIGO grading criteria: grade 1, 2, and 3 tumours, respectively, exhibit ≤ 5%, 6–50%, and > 50% solid non-glandular, non-squamous growth. The presence of severe cytological atypia in the majority of cells (> 50%) increases the grade by one level, but serous carcinoma should be excluded in cases with nuclear atypia that is out of proportion to the architecture {21993268}. Binary grading {30550484} is recommended, whereby grade 1 and 2 tumours are classified as low-grade and grade 3 tumours as high-grade. In low-grade EEC, endometrioid differentiation can be diagnosed on routine histology. In high-grade tumours, squamous differentiation strongly favours EEC over other histological endometrial carcinoma types.

Immunohistochemistry

Low-grade EEC shows diffuse strong immunoreactivity for ER/PR and patchy positivity for p16. This profile can be used to differentiate it from endocervical adenocarcinoma, which typically shows diffuse p16 immunoreactivity and negativity for ER and PR (HPV-associated) or negativity for p16, ER, and PR (HPV-independent) {30550485}. High-grade EEC may be difficult to distinguish from serous endometrial carcinoma, but it is usually solid and shows less-pronounced nuclear pleomorphism. Diffuse high-grade atypia out of proportion to architectural features raises serous carcinoma as a possibility. Loss of immunoreactivity for ARID1A, PTEN, or one of the mismatch repair proteins favours high-grade EEC. Abnormal p53 expression is reported in 2–5% of low-grade and 20% of high-grade EECs {29505428; 10679651; 9744308}.

Lymphovascular invasion

Lymphovascular invasion is present in 5–15% of cases and is frequently associated with the microcystic, elongated, and fragmented (MELF) pattern of invasion and with mismatch repair deficiency {25279582}. Particular artefacts, such as displacement of tumour cells in spaces and retraction of tissue due to delayed fixation, may mimic lymphovascular invasion and should be excluded {29356713}.

The incorporation of well-established molecular parameters can sharply separate four biologically distinct EECs (see #10612Table #10612 and #16536Fig. #16536), adding relevant prognostic information (see #16537Fig. #16537) {27006490; 26172027; 29344951} [[León-Castillo A, de Boer SM, Powell ME, et al. Molecular classification of the PORTEC-3 trial for high-risk endometrial cancer: impact on prognosis and benefit from adjuvant therapy. J Clin Oncol. Forthcoming 2020.]]. The availability of surrogate markers for all molecular subtypes (targeted POLE sequencing; MSH6, PMS2, and p53 immunohistochemistry) facilitates adoption.

Essential: invasive endometrial carcinoma with endometrioid differentiation.

Desirable: some degree of squamous, secretory, or mucinous differentiation.

EEC is staged according to the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification (see TNM staging of tumours of the uterus – endometrium [[Brierley JD, Gospodarowicz MK, Wittekind C, editors. TNM classification of malignant tumours. 8th ed. Oxford (UK): Wiley-Blackwell; 2017.]]) and the FIGO staging system.

FIGO and UICC staging is based on depth of myometrial invasion (< 50% or ≥ 50%) and on endocervical stromal, adnexal, and lymph node involvement. Unequivocal lymphovascular invasion is used in treatment algorithms, and the distinction between focal and extensive lymphovascular invasion (≥ 5 vessels) may have prognostic significance {26049688; 28709703}. It has been demonstrated that synchronous endometrioid carcinomas of endometrium and ovaries are mostly clonally related {26832770; 26832771}. Their indolent behaviour supports {24300466} conservative management when the following four criteria are met: (1) both tumours are low-grade, (2) < 50% myometrial invasion, (3) no involvement of any other site, and (4) absence of extensive lymphovascular invasion at any location {30723764}. For treatment purposes, these neoplasm should be managed as independent tumours. The efficacy of conservative treatment of grade 1 endometrioid carcinoma or endometrial atypical hyperplasia / endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia with hormonal agents may be monitored by histology, but this is not yet standard clinical practice {31846531}.
